h1: Kvass: the bread beer and how to make one in an Indian kitchen
title: Kvass: Bread Beer at Home in India | Craft Beer School
desc: What kvass is, how this low-alcohol bread drink is traditionally made and a simple method for brewing it in an Indian kitchen with safe bottling.
teaser: Stale bread, water, sugar and a pinch of yeast. Kvass is the easiest fermented drink you will ever make.
standfirst: Kvass is a lightly fermented drink made from bread, popular for centuries across Russia, Ukraine and Eastern Europe. It is sour-sweet, very low in alcohol and easy to make at home. Here is what it is and how to brew it in an Indian kitchen without a single piece of brewing kit.
sections:
Kvass is made by soaking dark bread, usually rye, in water, then fermenting the liquid with yeast and sugar. The result is a brown, slightly sweet, slightly sour drink with a bready flavour and a light fizz. It is traditionally very low in alcohol, usually below about 1.5% ABV. It is often sold from street barrels in summer in Eastern Europe.

It sits in a grey area between soft drink and beer. Commercial versions are often sweetened and barely alcoholic. Homemade kvass can drift higher if fermentation runs long, which is worth keeping in mind. Think of it as a cousin of kanji, the fermented black carrot drink many North Indian homes make in winter: a sour, living drink made from everyday ingredients.
Why it suits an Indian kitchen

Most Indian kitchens already have what kvass needs. Bread, sugar, a jar and a warm room. Indian heat, which makes beer brewing difficult, speeds kvass up: what takes two or three days in a cool European kitchen may take a day here. You do not need a fermenter, a hydrometer or temperature control. Our guide to brewing in a small apartment covers the space side if you want to go further later.

• About 500 g dark rye bread, or the darkest wholemeal bread you can find. Many Indian bakeries sell rye or multigrain loaves.
  • About 4 litres of drinking water, boiled.
  • About 100 to 150 g sugar, or jaggery for a deeper flavour.
  • A quarter teaspoon of dried baker's yeast.
  • A small handful of raisins (optional), plus mint or lemon if you like.

1. Slice the bread and toast it until dark brown but not burnt. The toasting gives kvass its colour and roasty flavour.
  2. Put the toast in a large clean steel pot or glass jar. Pour over the water, just off the boil. Cover and leave it to steep for 6 to 8 hours.
  3. Strain through a clean cloth, squeezing gently. You should have a brown, bread-scented liquid.
  4. Stir in the sugar or jaggery until dissolved. Let the liquid cool to room temperature.
  5. Sprinkle in the yeast, stir, cover loosely and leave at room temperature. In Indian summer heat around 30 °C, 12 to 24 hours is often enough. Taste it: you want light sourness and some fizz with sweetness still present.
  6. Bottle with a raisin or two in each bottle, close tightly and leave at room temperature for a few hours to build fizz, then refrigerate.

The one real danger in kvass is pressure. Yeast keeps working in a sealed bottle and the CO2 has nowhere to go. In Indian heat that happens fast. Bottles can burst. Glass is the worst material for it.

Use plastic PET soft drink bottles. Squeeze one after a few hours: once it feels firm, move all the bottles to the fridge. Cold slows the yeast almost to a stop. Drink within a week or so and open carefully over a sink. Our guide on bottle conditioning explains the same principle for beer.

Short, cool fermentation keeps kvass close to non-alcoholic. Longer or warmer fermentation raises alcohol and sourness. If anyone drinking it avoids alcohol entirely, keep the ferment short and refrigerate early. Rules around home fermentation vary by state in India, so check what applies where you live.

Clean everything well: pot, jar, cloth and bottles. Throw out any batch with fuzzy mould, a slimy texture or a sharp, solvent smell. Good kvass smells of toasted bread and fruit.

Once you have made a plain batch, try variations. Mint and lemon peel give a fresh summer version. A few slices of ginger add warmth. Jaggery in place of sugar gives a deeper, caramel note that suits the toasted bread. Some people add a handful of berries or beetroot for colour. Change one thing per batch so you learn what each addition does.

Kvass is a gentle introduction to fermentation. It teaches you how yeast behaves, how temperature changes speed and how sugar turns into fizz and flavour, the same lessons that sit at the heart of brewing beer.
faqs: Traditional kvass is very low in alcohol, usually below about 1.5% ABV. Longer or warmer fermentation can make it stronger, so keep the ferment short if you want it close to non-alcoholic.
Can I make kvass with regular white bread?
You can, but the flavour and colour will be weaker. Dark rye or wholemeal bread gives the classic brown colour and roasty, bready taste.
How long does homemade kvass keep?
About a week in the fridge. Keep it cold to slow the yeast and release pressure carefully when opening.
